newsitem.title: UK: P&O, Nedlloyd boxship merger details.
newsitem.headline: P&O, Nedlloyd boxship merger details.

text.p: Following are the key financial and operational points of the 50/50 global container shipping merger announced on Monday by Britain's P&O and Dutch Nedlloyd:

* The plan is seen having far-reaching implications for both Peninsular & Oriental Steam Navigation Company and Nedlloyd NV -- diverisified groups which have struggled for years to make reasonable returns from these expensive ships and other assets.
* P&O Nedlloyd may well expand further at a later date, the parents say, to take in other container lines seeking economies of scale. If it expands an IPO cannot be ruled out, they add.
* Nedlloyd will make a one-off balancing payment of $175 million to P&O reflecting the greater proportion of P&O assets in the venture.
* P&O Nedlloyd will take on the debt for its incoming assets and have initial net borrowings of $500 million.
* Savings over $200 million a year are seen from an annual cost base of $3.9 billion, but the firm also expects an initial restructuring overhead of about $100 million.
* The savings will come from staff reductions ($130 million), container operations ($20 million), vessel operations ($20 million) and other synergies ($30 million)
* About 1,400 staff from the combined workforce of 7,300 onshore and 2,100 at sea will be let go, of which about 250 redundancies will be in Britain and 300 in the Netherlands.

* The merged group will have a fleet of 112 owned and chartered ships, 540,000 teu of leased and owned containers and sees initial annual turnover of nearly $4.0 billion. * Nedlloyd sees the move as part of bid to achieve a 10 percent rate of return on its business, and says it will boost value to shareholders.
* The Dutch transport group's debt equity/ratio will rise to 63 percent after the deal from 57 percent before it.
* P&O is struggling to get its return on capital employed up to a level where shareholders will finally get some appreciation in their stock price and sees the deal as a key strategic move.
* P&O Containers was making a return of about 5.0 percent alone, but once in P&O Nedlloyd should produce a return of 13.5 percent, rising to 15 percent when geared into P&O's books.
* P&O Nedlloyd will have the world's biggest fleet in terms of container capacity (measured in twenty foot equivalent units or teus), but will be number three by volume carried.
* It will have global reach but is not yet what Nedlloyd calls a "mega-carrier" and will still need long-term partners.
* With its annual container volumes starting at about 2.5 million teus, the volume would have to grow towards 4.0 or 5.0 million teus to meet the mega-carrier ambition, Nedlloyd says.
* The parent firms expect national and Brussels competition regulators to support the move as "good for Europe".
* According to its chief executive, Briton Tim Harris, the new line will try to build up a fleet of efficient 6,600 teu liner ships and displace smaller ships out of the trunk fleet.
* Two options held by P&O to build new large boxships are being taken over by P&O Nedlloyd and turned into fixed orders, with two more options added immediately.
* P&O Nedlloyd will enter into full operation as soon as possible but not later than December 31, 1996.
* It will be a British-based company but with its European operations and all ship operations based in Rotterdam.
